News / NewsBTC / Zcash Whale Wakes Up After 9 Years, Moves $11.39 Million To Kraken

Zcash Whale Wakes Up After 9 Years, Moves $11.39 Million To Kraken 3 min read

ZECUSD Key takeaways Lookonchain reports a Zcash whale moved 15,750 ZEC, about $11.39 million, to Kraken after nine years. The whale reportedly bought 23,412 ZEC in 2017 at about $215 (just over $5 million). The deposit is roughly two-thirds of that position. At about $723 per ZEC, the coins are worth around $8 million more than their estimated cost, a gain of roughly 236%. A deposit to an exchange is not proof of a sale, and the acquisition price is an estimate, not a verified record. More early holders moving dormant coins to exchanges could mean new Zcash buyers absorb supply from older holders. Nine years is an eternity in crypto. Yet one Zcash whale appears to have spent that long sitting on an investment made during the privacy coin’s early days. On Thursday, blockchain monitoring platform Lookonchain reported that the investor had moved 15,750 ZEC, worth $11.39 million, to Kraken. The coins date back to 2017, when Ethereum was still a relatively young network, decentralized finance barely existed and Zcash was attempting to establish itself as a more private alternative to Bitcoin. Almost a decade later, the wallet is active again. And its owner’s reported acquisition price makes the transaction particularly interesting.

A $5 Million Bet On Zcash In 2017 According to Lookonchain, the whale originally acquired 23,412 ZEC at an average price of approximately $215, representing an investment of just over $5 million. The latest transactions account for roughly two-thirds of that original position, with at least 7,750 ZEC transferred to a Kraken deposit address.

At the reported transfer valuation of approximately $723 per ZEC, those 15,750 coins are worth around $8 million more than their estimated acquisition cost. That would represent a return of approximately 236% if the investor sold them at that price.

What makes this wallet fascinating, however, is what happened between those two valuations. Zcash spent much of 2024 and early 2025 trading around $16 to $20 before staging a remarkable comeback. At $20 per coin, the whale’s original investment would have been worth less than $470,000, a paper loss of more than 90%, assuming the position remained intact. Holding an asset through a temporary market correction is one thing. Holding it through years of declining relevance, while newer cryptocurrencies attract developers, investors and attention, is something else entirely. Whatever the owner’s reasons for keeping the coins untouched, the decision has aged considerably better than it appeared to during Zcash’s quieter years. The Interesting Paradox Behind A Zcash Whale There is something almost ironic about the fact that investors are following the movements of a whale holding one of crypto’s best-known privacy coins. Unlike networks where transaction privacy is mandatory, Zcash supports both transparent and shielded transactions. Transparent addresses allow observers to examine balances and transfers, while shielded transactions use zero-knowledge cryptography to conceal transaction details. That distinction explains how blockchain monitoring platforms can identify certain large ZEC movements despite the cryptocurrency’s privacy capabilities. It also explains why the available information tells only part of the story. Lookonchain can identify an apparent exchange deposit and estimate its value. Establishing who controls the wallet, whether ownership changed privately during those nine years or what the investor intends to do next is considerably harder. Even the reported acquisition price is an estimate rather than a verified record of the owner’s personal trading history. That is an important limitation of on-chain analysis, particularly when dealing with a network explicitly designed to give users greater control over their financial visibility. Zcash’s Comeback Has Given Early Investors An Exit The renewed enthusiasm surrounding Zcash has attracted a different kind of investor from the one buying ZEC in 2017. Corporate treasury strategies have emerged, institutional investors have taken an interest in privacy-focused assets, and the debate over financial surveillance has given Zcash a fresh investment narrative. NewsBTC previously reported that Winklevoss Capital backed the launch of a dedicated Zcash treasury strategy, illustrating how exposure to the cryptocurrency has begun extending beyond traditional crypto wallets. But the revival of an old cryptocurrency also comes with an interesting complication: investors who have spent years underwater finally have an opportunity to recover their capital or take profits. That does not necessarily make the Kraken deposit bearish. A transfer to an exchange is not proof of a completed sale, and one wallet cannot establish a broader trend among Zcash holders. Still, the transaction is worth watching. If more early investors start moving dormant coins onto exchanges, Zcash’s new buyers may find themselves absorbing supply from an entirely different generation of holders. Nine years ago, someone reportedly committed more than $5 million to the idea of private digital money. Today, the blockchain offers a glimpse of what that investment has become. Whether the owner has finished holding Zcash is a question the blockchain alone cannot yet answer.

item.content:encoded:

‘Carl Icahn Did Not Play Nice:’ Michael Dell Takes a Swipe at Billionaire as Activist Investor’s Fortune Reportedly Shrinks by $21 Billion 2 min read

DELL IEP CVI Michael Dell took a pointed swipe at billionaire activist investor Carl Icahn , reviving memories of their bitter corporate battle more than a decade ago as Icahn’s fortune reportedly dwindles amid mounting financial pressures. The Dell Technologies Inc. DELL founder appeared to reference their 2013 showdown. The remark came after Bloomberg reported that Icahn’s wealth had fallen to roughly $1.3 billion, down about $21 billion over the past five years. Dell Takes a Swipe at Icahn “Carl Icahn did not play nice and he did not win,” Dell wrote in a post on X .

Michael Dell 🇺🇸 @MichaelDell

Carl Icahn did not play nice and he did not win #PlayNiceButWin

Nov 25, 2026

The post appeared to reference Dell’s 2021 memoir, "Play Nice But Win: A CEO’s Journey From Founder to Leader," which recounts his efforts to take his namesake company private and rebuild its business away from the pressures of quarterly earnings expectations. The 2013 confrontation pitted Dell’s plan to take the company private against Icahn’s alternative proposal. The activist investor opposed the buyout and pushed for a transaction involving a substantial share repurchase and warrants that would give shareholders exposure to future gains. Dell ultimately secured shareholder approval for the $24.9 billion buyout in Sept. 2013, taking the company private with financial backing from Silver Lake and other investors. The transaction was completed a month later. Carl Icahn did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comment. Icahn’s Fortune Under Pressure Icahn’s wealth reportedly peaked at $26.1 billion in December 2013, when he ranked among the world’s 25 richest people. The pressure has intensified around Icahn Enterprises LP IEP , his publicly traded investment partnership. The company warned in its third-quarter (Q3) results that there was no assurance it could refinance $1.4 billion in bonds due in May on acceptable terms. Shares of CVR Energy Inc. CVI , a major IEP holding, have also dropped roughly 40% since the refiner agreed to acquire two additional refineries earlier this month. The History Behind Dell and Icahn’s Feud The two billionaires’ rivalry dates back to 2013, when Dell sought to take his company private in a deal valued at approximately $24.9 billion. Icahn emerged as a prominent opponent, arguing that shareholders would be better served by an alternative plan involving a large stock buyback and warrants. Icahn also challenged the buyout through public statements and legal action, while Dell argued that taking the company private would give it the flexibility to pursue a longer-term transformation. Dell’s buyout eventually went through, and the company began its transformation as a private enterprise. In 2016, Dell acquired EMC in a $67 billion transaction, expanding beyond its traditional PC business into enterprise storage and infrastructure. The company subsequently returned to public markets in December 2018, with its shares beginning regular trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker DELL. item.title: Bitcoin’s Recovery Faces a New Warning After $2 Billion in ETF Outflows
item.description: Key takeawaysThe Bitcoin recovery above $60,000 is offering some relief after a brutal November sell-off, but the money flowing through US spot Bitcoin ETFs tells a less encouraging story. The funds ...
item.content:encoded:
News / NewsBTC / Bitcoin’s Recovery Faces a New Warning After $2 Billion in ETF Outflows

Bitcoin’s Recovery Faces a New Warning After $2 Billion in ETF Outflows 4 min read

BTCUSD Key takeaways US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $2.05 billion in combined net outflows over four straight sessions ending November 24, per Farside Investors, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for roughly $1.77 billion. Bitcoin is back above $60,000 after trading as low as about $55,300 on November 21, according to Glassnode. Reclaiming $60,000 does not by itself confirm the correction is over: holders who bought near that level may sell into the rebound. Bitcoin trades far beyond US ETFs, so outflows are not proof of further downside, but a recovery that holds despite redemptions would be a stronger signal. Thanksgiving closes US markets, so the missing ETF data is not a sign of improved demand. Friday’s session will be more telling. The Bitcoin recovery above $60,000 is offering some relief after a brutal November sell-off, but the money flowing through US spot Bitcoin ETFs tells a less encouraging story. The funds recorded more than $2 billion in combined net outflows over four consecutive trading sessions ending November 24. Bitcoin’s return to the psychologically important price level follows a difficult week in which the cryptocurrency traded as low as approximately $55,300. The rebound is welcome. What is less clear is whether buyers have returned with enough capital to sustain it. Bitcoin ETFs Are Still Losing Money The scale of the recent withdrawals deserves more attention than the recovery itself. According to Farside Investors, US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded net outflows of $582.3 million on November 19, followed by another $669.2 million the next day. Withdrawals continued on Monday and Tuesday, bringing the combined total across those four trading sessions to approximately $2.05 billion. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for roughly $1.77 billion in net outflows during that period.

Wednesday’s figures are still subject to final reporting confirmation, although available data points to further withdrawals. These numbers do not mean that every institutional investor is abandoning Bitcoin. ETF shareholders include different types of investors, from financial advisers and asset managers to individual traders. Some may be reducing risk, while others could be unwinding positions that were never intended as long-term investments. What the figures establish is that the ETF market has experienced persistent net redemptions, even after Bitcoin’s substantial decline. That is not the response bulls would ideally want to see from buyers following a major correction. Bitcoin’s Drop Below $60,000 Exposed a Deeper Problem Earlier this week, Bitcoin fell below $60,000 again after an initial recovery above $64,000 failed to hold. Glassnode’s November 24 report, titled The Canary in the Coal Mine, documented the severity of Bitcoin’s latest decline. The cryptocurrency reached approximately $55,300 on November 21, falling beneath the lows established during the summer. That matters because investors who bought during previous corrections may now be sitting on losses despite having entered the market at what appeared to be relatively attractive prices. Glassnode’s historical data reveals another uncomfortable detail. Long-term holders recently accounted for more than 75% of Bitcoin’s realized losses before their share fell back toward 50%. Similar periods of selling at a loss appeared during previous bear markets, although that alone does not establish that Bitcoin has reached a bottom.

Their behavior becomes particularly important when Bitcoin starts recovering. Some holders may use a rebound to reduce their exposure or exit positions closer to their original purchase price. Others may be willing to hold through further volatility. Which group dominates will influence how much buying is required to sustain the next move higher. A price that previously attracted buyers can become an area of selling pressure when the market approaches it from below. This is one reason why reclaiming $60,000 should not automatically be interpreted as confirmation that the correction has ended. A Market Bottom Does Not Require Everyone to Turn Bullish There is a credible argument against interpreting persistent ETF outflows as evidence that Bitcoin must fall further. Markets can begin recovering before investor sentiment improves. In fact, waiting for every major indicator to turn positive can mean missing a substantial portion of a reversal. Glassnode’s latest research offers some historical perspective. Bitcoin’s realized losses relative to capital inflows over the preceding year have reached their highest intensity since the FTX collapse in 2022. Previous episodes of heavy losses have occurred near major market bottoms, but severe selling alone is not enough to confirm that a recovery is underway.

Bitcoin also trades across a much broader market than US exchange-traded funds. Direct purchases, overseas exchanges and other investment vehicles can absorb selling even when American funds experience redemptions. The distinction is between evidence that a market can recover and evidence that it has already established a sustainable recovery. Bitcoin’s latest bounce demonstrates that buyers are willing to step in at lower prices. It does not yet establish whether those buyers can absorb additional selling at higher levels. If Bitcoin begins to hold its gains despite persistent ETF withdrawals, that would itself be an encouraging development. It would suggest that demand elsewhere in the market is capable of offsetting some of the pressure coming from the funds. For now, the price and ETF data leave that question open. Thanksgiving Could Make Bitcoin’s Next Move Harder to Read Thursday’s Thanksgiving holiday adds another complication to the recovery. US equity markets are closed, removing a regular trading session for American spot Bitcoin ETFs while cryptocurrency exchanges continue operating. The absence of new ETF flow figures during the holiday should not be confused with an improvement in institutional demand. With fewer traditional financial market participants active, Bitcoin’s immediate price movements may also provide an incomplete picture of how investors are responding to the recent sell-off. Friday’s shortened US trading session and the subsequent return to normal market hours will provide more useful evidence. For traders, the important signals are whether Bitcoin can retain its recent gains, whether ETF redemptions begin to ease and whether buying remains strong enough to absorb selling when normal market participation resumes. The $60,000 level may dominate the headlines, but the more convincing recovery will be the one that can survive without depending entirely on temporary relief from selling pressure.
